questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement with lopsided margins
questions.stem: Why can Cohen's kappa be low even when two coders agree often, when category margins are skewed?

answer.exemplar: Skewed margins inflate expected agreement by chance, so observed agreement must exceed a high baseline; kappa can therefore stay low despite high raw agreement.

questions.explanation: Kappa subtracts chance agreement. Lopsided categories raise chance agreement, shrinking kappa even with many matches.
questions.hint: Kappa corrects for chance, which rises with skew.

questions.stem: If one new code appears after five no-new-code interviews, what is the new-code rate per interview across those six?
questions.explanation: One new code across six interviews is about 0.1667 per interview. The low rate supports, but does not prove, saturation.
questions.hint: Divide new codes by total interviews.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Coverage of a joint display
questions.learningObjective: Mark missing data in a joint display

stimulus.body: A joint display has 10 rows. Two rows show a quantitative score with no matching quote, and one row shows a quote with no score.

questions.stem: How should the display handle these gaps?

options.text: Delete the three incomplete rows
Leave the cells empty and annotate the gaps
Fill gaps with the nearest row's values
Merge the three rows into one

questions.explanation: Empty, annotated cells document missing data honestly. Deleting or imputing distorts the display.
questions.hint: Annotate gaps, do not hide them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Counting theme instances at the unit of analysis
questions.stem: A report says a theme appears in 12 instances; the unit is the participant. What does 12 mean?

options.text: Twelve participants mentioned the theme
Twelve separate mentions occurred
options.misconception: confuses participant unit with mention count

options.text: Twelve focus groups mentioned the theme
Twelve percent of participants mentioned it

questions.explanation: With participant as unit, 12 means 12 participants. Mentions, groups, and percentages are different metrics.
questions.hint: Read the count with its unit.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement with lopsided margins
questions.stem: When margins are lopsided, which approach best supplements Cohen's kappa?

options.text: Report kappa alone and ignore the margins
Report kappa with prevalence-adjusted kappa and margins
Switch to raw percent agreement only
Use Pearson correlation instead

questions.explanation: Reporting kappa with prevalence-adjusted kappa and margins gives a fuller picture under skew.
questions.hint: Pair kappa with prevalence-adjusted kappa.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a saturation claim commits you to
questions.stem: A saturation claim commits the researcher to which of the following?

options.text: That no further sampling could ever yield new themes
That the sample was adequate for the studied context
That the codebook is complete for all populations
That future studies need not sample again

questions.explanation: Saturation commits to adequacy in context, not universal completeness. Overstating it misleads readers.
questions.hint: Saturation is a local adequacy claim.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Discarding singleton codes
questions.stem: What rule of thumb helps decide whether to keep a singleton code?

answer.exemplar: Keep a singleton when it is relevant to the research question and supported by a rich, credible extract; otherwise discard it with documentation.

questions.explanation: Relevance and evidence guide retention. Frequency alone is not the deciding factor.
questions.hint: Relevance and evidence decide retention.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: How widespread a theme is across interviews
questions.stem: In subgroup X, 6 of 10 interviews mention a theme; in subgroup Y, 4 of 10. What is the difference in percentage points?
questions.explanation: Sixty percent minus forty percent is twenty percentage points. The difference is descriptive, not necessarily significant.
questions.hint: Subtract the two percentages.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Share of talk time in a focus group

stimulus.body: A pie chart shows talk-time shares of 50%, 20%, 15%, 10%, and 5% across five participants in a focus group.

questions.stem: What is the combined share of the two largest participants?

options.text: 70% of total talk time
50% of total talk time
35% of total talk time
20% of total talk time

questions.explanation: Fifty plus twenty is seventy percent. The combined share highlights dominance by two voices.
questions.hint: Add the two largest shares.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Unequal sample sizes across mixed phases
questions.stem: Why might a mixed study use 200 survey respondents and only 15 interviewees?

options.text: Because the survey needs breadth and interviews need depth
Because interviews are less important than surveys
Because 15 is the maximum for qualitative work
Because surveys are cheaper to run

questions.explanation: Surveys seek breadth and interviews seek depth, so sizes differ. Cost and importance are secondary.
questions.hint: Breadth versus depth.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Extracts with no majority code
questions.stem: When an extract has no majority code, what should the write-up emphasise?

options.text: The absence of a dominant theme and its analytic meaning
The most frequent code as if it were dominant
The extract's removal from the dataset
A new blended code for that extract

questions.explanation: Emphasise the absence of dominance and its meaning. Forcing, deleting, or blending distorts the data.
questions.hint: Report ambiguity as a finding.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: New codes per interview after the plateau
questions.stem: New codes per interview fall from 5 to 1 to 0 over three blocks; what trend does this show?

options.text: Approaching saturation of the codebook
Interviews are getting shorter
options.misconception: blames length for a coding trend

options.text: Coders are becoming fatigued
The topic is exhausted and no more data matter

questions.explanation: A declining new-code rate signals approaching saturation. It does not prove completion or blame data quality.
questions.hint: Decline signals saturation.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Coverage of a joint display
questions.stem: How should a researcher evaluate whether a joint display has adequate coverage?

answer.exemplar: Check that each case has data for both strands where expected, flag missing cells, and justify any gaps by the study design.

questions.explanation: Adequate coverage means documented presence or justified absence across strands. Gaps must be visible and explained.
questions.hint: Document presence or justified absence.

questions.topic: Counting theme instances at the unit of analysis
questions.learningObjective: Report a count with its unit
questions.stem: A theme is present in 8 of 10 focus groups; how many groups support it?
questions.explanation: Eight groups support the theme when the group is the unit. Mention counts would be a different number.
questions.hint: Count groups, not mentions.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement with lopsided margins

stimulus.body: Two coders agree on 90% of cases. One category dominates at 85% of all cases. Cohen's kappa is 0.35.

questions.stem: What does this pattern indicate?

options.text: Agreement is poor and coders need retraining
Kappa is depressed by skewed margins
Raw agreement should replace kappa
The dominant category should be split

questions.explanation: Skewed margins inflate chance agreement, depressing kappa. The low kappa reflects skew, not necessarily poor coding.
questions.hint: Skew depresses kappa.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a saturation claim commits you to
questions.stem: Which claim is most defensible for a saturated sample?

options.text: The sample was adequate for this study's question
No new themes exist anywhere on this topic
The codebook is final and immutable
Future studies need not sample again

questions.explanation: Saturation supports adequacy for this study. It does not prove universality, finality, or transfer to future work.
questions.hint: Keep the claim local and modest.
